clinicalScope: Bile as the hepatic secretory fluid in adults, with emphasis on its physiology, disorders and clinical relevance in low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Bile Physiology and Clinical Correlates
subject: Physiology
summary: Bile is a watery, alkaline fluid made by the liver that helps digest fats and removes waste. Understanding how it is formed, stored and flows is key to diagnosing jaundice, gallstones and cholestasis, especially where imaging is limited.

sections.p: Bile maintains lipid digestion, cholesterol balance and excretion of bilirubin and drugs. Its production and flow are tightly regulated to keep serum bilirubin and cholesterol within normal limits.
b: Composed of water (≈97%), bile salts, phospholipids, bilirubin, cholesterol and electrolytes.
Secreted continuously by hepatocytes into canaliculi, then collected in intra‑hepatic ducts.
Stored and concentrated in the gallbladder; released on CCK stimulus after a fatty meal.
Enterohepatic circulation recycles >95% of bile salts via the terminal ileum.

sections.p: The liver converts cholesterol to primary bile acids, conjugates them, and secretes them into bile.
b: Cholesterol → 7α‑hydroxylase → cholic & chenodeoxycholic acids.
Conjugation with glycine or taurine increases solubility.
Bile salts form micelles that emulsify dietary fats.
Phospholipid (lecithin) protects cholangiocyte membranes from detergent injury.

sections.p: Hepatocytes use specific transporters to move bile components across membranes.
b: Bile salt export pump (BSEP) moves conjugated bile acids into canaliculi.
Multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP2) exports bilirubin glucuronides and phosphatidylcholine.
Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase maintains the osmotic gradient that draws water into bile.
Tight junctions prevent back‑leak of bile into the sinusoidal blood.

sections.p: Bile synthesis is modulated by hormonal and neural signals that reflect dietary intake and systemic needs.
b: Cholecystokinin (CCK) triggers gallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation.
Fibroblast growth factor 19 (FGF19) released from ileal enterocytes down‑regulates CYP7A1, reducing bile‑acid synthesis.
Secretin stimulates bicarbonate‑rich hepatic secretion, diluting bile when the duodenum is acidic.
Autocrine feedback: high intra‑hepatic bile‑acid concentrations inhibit CYP7A1 transcription.

sections.p: Bile links the liver, gallbladder, pancreas and intestine in digestion and waste elimination.
b: Pancreatic enzymes mix with bile in the duodenum to complete fat hydrolysis.
Ileal bile‑acid receptors (FXR) regulate glucose and lipid metabolism systemically.
Renal excretion of bilirubin metabolites occurs only after intestinal conversion to urobilinogen.
In cholestasis, retained bile acids can cause pruritus via skin nerve activation.

sections.p: Several physiological and environmental factors modify bile composition and flow.
b: High‑fat meals increase CCK release, augmenting gallbladder emptying.
Prolonged fasting reduces gallbladder contractility, predisposing to sludge.
Ileal resection (>50 %) markedly lowers bile‑acid pool, causing fat malabsorption.
Herbal remedies containing sennosides can irritate the gallbladder wall.

sections.p: Disruption of bile formation, flow or reabsorption produces jaundice, gallstones and cholestatic liver disease.
b: Obstructive (post‑hepatic) blockage – gallstones, strictures, tumors.
Intra‑hepatic cholestasis – drug‑induced (e.g., rifampicin), viral hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis.
Impaired bile‑acid synthesis – genetic CYP7A1 deficiency, extensive ileal loss.
Gallbladder hypomotility – fasting, diabetes, autonomic neuropathy.

sections.p: Symptoms arise from impaired fat digestion, bilirubin accumulation or bile‑acid toxicity.
b: Jaundice: yellow sclerae, skin; dark urine, pale stools.
Pruritus: especially on palms and soles, worsens at night.
Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals (biliary colic).
Steatorrhea and fat‑soluble vitamin deficiency in chronic cholestasis.

sections.p: Laboratory and bedside tests identify the level and cause of biliary disturbance.

t.b: Distinguishes conjugated (post‑hepatic) from unconjugated (pre‑hepatic) rise; direct >20 µmol/L suggests obstruction.
Elevated in cholestasis; GGT helps differentiate hepatic from bone ALP rise.
Detects gallstones, ductal dilation, gallbladder wall thickening.
Markedly raised in intra‑hepatic cholestasis; guides severity.

sections.p: Applying physiology to bedside decisions improves patient outcomes in low‑resource settings.
b: In a patient with jaundice and normal ALP, consider hemolysis rather than biliary disease.
When ultrasound shows a solitary stone <5 mm, expect spontaneous passage; monitor for pain resolution.
Use oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) to improve bile flow in primary biliary cholangitis when steroids are unavailable.
Educate patients on low‑fat diet and regular meals to prevent gallbladder stasis.

sections.p: Clarify frequent errors that can mislead diagnosis or management.
b: Bile is not the same as pancreatic juice – it contains bile salts, not digestive enzymes.
Normal serum bilirubin does not rule out early acute cholecystitis; clinical exam remains vital.
Absence of urobilinogen in urine does not always mean obstruction; severe liver failure can also suppress production.
Gallbladder mucus is clear; bile’s colour comes from bilirubin pigments.

sections.p: Strategic steps to answer exam questions on bile physiology and disease.
b: Identify the level of jaundice (pre‑, intra‑, post‑hepatic) using bilirubin fractions.
Correlate ALP/GGT pattern with imaging to localise obstruction.
Recall the enterohepatic circulation steps to explain effects of ileal resection.
Select UDCA for cholestatic disorders when steroids are contraindicated.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe right upper quadrant pain with fever → possible acute cholangitis.
Progressive jaundice with mental status change → hepatic encephalopathy.
Pruritus with bilirubin >300 µmol/L → risk of skin breakdown and infection.

faq.q: Why does gallstone disease increase after fasting?
faq.a: Fasting reduces CCK release, leading to gallbladder stasis and supersaturation of cholesterol, promoting stone formation.

faq.q: Can bile salts be measured directly?
faq.a: Serum bile‑acid assays exist but are rarely needed; ALP and GGT are practical surrogates for cholestasis.
UDCA is considered safe and is used for intra‑hepatic cholestasis of pregnancy when benefits outweigh theoretical risks.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with jaundice, dark urine and normal ALP – what is the most likely mechanism? — Predominant unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from hemolysis; bilirubin production exceeds hepatic conjugation capacity.

You have a patient with right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal, ultrasound shows a 4 mm stone in the cystic duct. What is the next best step? — Observe and provide analgesia; most stones <5 mm pass spontaneously, schedule follow‑up ultrasound.
Explain why serum bilirubin may be normal in early acute cholecystitis. — Bile flow is still intact; inflammation is confined to the gallbladder wall without obstructing the common duct.

A patient with HIV on protease inhibitors develops pruritus and cholestatic LFTs. Which drug class should be added and why? — Ursodeoxycholic acid to improve bile flow and reduce bile‑acid toxicity; steroids are avoided due to infection risk.
How does extensive ileal resection affect fat absorption? — Loss of bile‑acid reabsorption reduces the enterohepatic pool, leading to insufficient micelle formation and steatorrhea.

Differentiate pre‑hepatic, intra‑hepatic and post‑hepatic jaundice using laboratory patterns. — Pre‑hepatic: ↑ indirect bilirubin, normal ALP/GGT; Intra‑hepatic: ↑ both direct bilirubin and ALP/GGT; Post‑hepatic: ↑ direct bilirubin with marked ALP/GGT elevation.
What bedside sign suggests gallbladder inflammation? — Positive Murphy’s sign: pain on inspiration when the examiner palpates the right subcostal area.

Why is GGT useful when ALP is elevated in a patient with suspected bone disease? — GGT is liver‑specific; a normal GGT with high ALP points to bone origin, whereas elevated GGT indicates hepatic cholestasis.

In a low‑resource clinic without ultrasound, how would you assess for biliary obstruction? — Look for jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier’s sign), and perform a focused abdominal exam for tenderness and Murphy’s sign.
What are the contraindications to using cholestyramine for pruritus in cholestasis? — Severe malabsorption, vitamin K deficiency, and patients on warfarin (it interferes with absorption).
